title: Vayechi: not in God's place (Genesis 50:15–21)
hookLine: Joseph refuses revenge: "ye meant evil against me; but God meant it for good"

cards: There's a particular fear that shows up after a funeral. The parent who held everyone together is gone, and old debts look different. Was my brother only being nice because Dad was watching?
Joseph's brothers feel exactly that. For seventeen years in Egypt, Joseph has fed and protected them. But now their father is buried, and they think: maybe he was just waiting.
Maybe now he'll pay us back for the pit and the sale. So they send him a message.

teach.b: The message says: before he died, your father told us to tell you, please forgive your brothers. The Torah never shows Jacob saying any such thing.
The Talmud concludes they made it up, and draws a surprising rule from it: you may soften the truth for the sake of peace. Joseph hears their words, and he cries.
Then the brothers come and throw themselves down: we're your slaves. Remember the dreams, the sheaves bowing, the stars bowing?
Here it is, finally, the brothers on the ground. Joseph could take it.

teach.h: AM I IN THE PLACE OF GOD?
teach.b: Instead he says, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Fear not; for am I in the place of God?" In Hebrew, ha-tachat Elohim ani. Am I standing where God stands?
Judging and punishing isn't my seat.

teach.h: YOU MEANT EVIL. HE MEANT GOOD.
teach.b: Then: "ye meant evil against me; but God meant it for good." He doesn't pretend. What they did was wrong, and he names it.
But he refuses to be the one who settles the account. He says he'll provide for them and their little ones, and the text says he comforted them and spoke to their hearts.
With that, the book of Genesis ends. Joseph dies at a hundred and ten, still in Egypt. When a congregation finishes reading a book of the Torah, it calls out together: chazak, chazak, v'nitchazek.
Be strong, be strong, and let us strengthen one another.

how: When the reading of a whole book of the Torah is completed in synagogue, the congregation says chazak, chazak, v'nitchazek; Jewish law also forbids taking revenge or bearing a grudge, from Leviticus 19:18.

o: and he wept, the brothers' fear after the funeral
and he forgave, Joseph's word to his brothers
and he lived, the portion that closes Genesis

s: Joseph told his brothers they had done nothing wrong
he said plainly, ye meant evil against me, and still refused to punish them.
the Torah shows Jacob asking Joseph to forgive his brothers
only the brothers' message says so; the Talmud concludes they invented it for peace.
Genesis ends with Joseph's death in Egypt
he dies at a hundred and ten, and the book closes.

games.q: you're Joseph. your father is buried. the brothers who sold you are lying at your feet, offering to be your slaves. what do you do?
o: accept; your dreams have come true.
tell them it's not your place to punish, and provide for them.
forgive them, but send them away.
games.why: Joseph said: fear not, am I in the place of God? you meant evil, God meant it for good. then he promised to feed them and their children, and comforted them.

practice: Bring to mind someone who has wronged you, and one way you could get even, even a small one: the pointed comment, the cold shoulder, the story you could tell about them.
Name the wrong honestly, like Joseph: they did that, it was wrong. Then imagine setting the payback down, because it isn't your seat, just for today.

wordCard.voice: Vayechi. The last portion of Genesis, which ends with Joseph refusing revenge: am I in the place of God?

orig.note: Hebrew: am I in the place of God? Joseph's answer to his brothers (Genesis 50:19).

carryVoice: Your line: not my place to punish. One book of the Torah closes here. Day two hundred twenty, done.
